questions.problem: Consider the finite region bounded by the curve $y={x}^{2}-{x}^{3}$ and the $x$-axis. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(1-x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are  $x=0$ and  $x=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x({x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x \\  & ={2\pi (\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\text{ }-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{5})-0] \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{20}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{10}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(3-x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=0$ and $x=3.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=3.$  

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}x(3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(3{x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238267/assets/780120c106065874c04d97b8b6ef10e3e81e1cf9fd7c7b19bc633963cbadafe4.png)

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $y=4x-2{x}^{2}$ and $y=2{x}^{3},$ as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $f(x)=4x-2{x}^{2}$ and $g(x)=2{x}^{3}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ 4x-2{x}^{2} & =2{x}^{3} \\ 4x-2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3} & =0 \\ -2x(-2+x+{x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x(x-1)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=-2,$ $x=0,$  and $x=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1$ because we are only concerned about $x\ge 0.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238267/assets/e695cfd83116df98b1530e2d53186de0ebcd03c6056c2b8d7c2272a76fbd790c.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=g(x)=2{x}^{3},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=f(x)=4x-2{x}^{2}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([\text{upper}]-[\text{lower}])\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x([4x-2{x}^{2}]-[2{x}^{3}])\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x(4x-2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $y=-{x}^{2}+2x+1$ and $y={x}^{2}+1,$ as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $f(x)=-{x}^{2}+2x+1$ and $g(x)={x}^{2}+1.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ -{x}^{2}+2x+1 & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ -2{x}^{2}+2x & =0 \\ -2x(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=0,$ and $x=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$  

Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238267/assets/8790ae667c9a2741e2a732ff69d9afe5633dc26df7b02eee52fb51478524282b.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=g(x)={x}^{2}+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=f(x)=-{x}^{2}+2x+1.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([\text{upper}]-[\text{lower}])\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x([-{x}^{2}+2x+1]-[{x}^{2}+1])\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x(2x-2{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(1-3x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=0$ and $x=\frac{1}{3}.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{1}{3}.$  

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/3}x(x-3{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/3}({x}^{2}-3{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4})|}_{0}^{1/3} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{1}{3\cdot {3}^{3}}-\frac{3}{4\cdot {3}^{4}})-0] \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{324}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{162}\end{aligned}
$$
